records.name: Nothern Cape
records.summary:
The single documented trans-specific violent incident in this dossier occurred here: on 14 May 2024 in Upington, 27-year-old transgender woman Jo-Ann Isaks was stabbed multiple times and her body set on fire in her own room, discovered by a family member who noticed the house burning. TGEU's Trans Day of Remembrance register records the killing and notes that "the LGBTIQ+ community in the Northern Cape has been shaken" - a province-level community response in a small province where one violent death is a meaningful rate observation. Police opened a murder case and reported no arrests at the time of the entry; the register records that police 'identified' the decedent by a deadname.

The killing is a lone incident and not clearly patterned or state-implicated; there is no evidence of impunity or victim-prosecution in the dossier, and no provincial legislative or enforcement finding against trans visitors. The score therefore reflects severity-dominant weighting: the method (burning) is extreme and the community-level shock signal is real, but the single-incident rule cautions against large score moves from an unpatterned crime. Northern Cape does not appear in the customary-authority / traditional-court geography and has no identified institutional climate finding.

records.name: Mpumalanga
records.summary:
Mpumalanga is where the country's official house of traditional leaders launched its organised campaign against constitutional equality for queer people. Meeting at Hazyview in June 2010, the National House of Traditional Leaders and its provincial houses — while professing to 'respect' the Constitutional Court's same-sex marriage judgment — resolved that 'traditional leaders are disappointed that this immoral practice has been given a lifeline by our courts', declared their opposition to legal recognition, warned of ostracism and violence, and vowed a five-year campaign against it. Reporting in 2016 documented the same body asking Parliament to review the constitutional clause that protects people from discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.

This is official traditional-structure hostility, taken on this province's soil and stated as durable climate rather than enacted law: there is no provincial statute against queer people, no enforcement against visitors, and no retrieved Mpumalanga-specific trans-incident series. The finding is the platform the country's chiefhood announced here — and did not retract.

records.name: Limpopo
records.summary:
Limpopo's rural life runs through chiefs and traditional courts to a degree that makes the parallel customary-law system the province's defining risk factor. Human Rights Watch's analysis of the legislation at issue warned that it 'establishes a separate legal system for people living in the former Bantustans' and 'threatens to undermine this security for millions of South Africans living in rural areas', 'particularly for the exercise of gender and sexual rights' — because chiefs and traditional courts adjudicate personal-status and morality-adjacent matters under customary law, with a consent presumption running against the individual. The later record, from a 2025 verification pass: the bill was enacted as the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act of 2019, and was then declared unconstitutional by the Constitutional Court in 2023, with the declaration suspended and the Act's validity extended while Parliament works on a replacement. A 2012 activist report — 'culture of the chiefs threatens our rights' — pressed the same case contemporaneously.

No statute criminalises a visitor's expression here and no trans-specific incident series is recorded. But for an outed visitor in rural Limpopo, the practical moral authority is often the chief's court rather than the ordinary court — and that jurisdiction's record on gender and sexuality runs against the individual. The absence of recorded incidents reflects under-reporting, not demonstrated safety.

freshness.fact: Chiefs/customary-court authority issue remains live: Constitutional Court (CCT73/22, 2023) invalidated parts of the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act but suspended the declaration pending fix; 2012-era sources remain directionally current, not superseded.

records.name: North West
records.summary:
North West sits squarely in the former-Bantustan geography where the traditional-courts jurisdiction is most extensive following the Bantustan-era map: HRW's analysis of the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act identifies these areas as a "separate legal system" whose adjudication of gender and sexual matters under customary law with a consent presumption against the individual constitutes the principal sub-national legal divergence in South Africa. The Act was declared invalid in Mogale (2023) but suspended and extended; the replacement Bill (TKLB) has been delayed. No province has religious criminal law; no statute criminalises a visitor's expression here.

North West is also the only province outside Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and the Western Cape to have received its own representative hate-crime prevalence study (2010; the GALA-hosted Love Not Hate review records only three quantitative studies ever attempted nationally), giving it a data-presence signal: incidents against queer people here are, historically, more likely to appear in research rather than only in the "dark figure" of unreported crime that characterises most provinces. No trans-specific incident series was found. The 2010 study covers gay and lesbian people; its relevance to a trans visitor is as a proxy for reporting culture and the volume of anti-queer violence in a traditional-authority-heavy province.

records.name: Eastern Cape
records.summary:
The Eastern Cape is listed among the former-Bantustan provinces where traditional-court jurisdiction operates—HRW's analysis of the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act identifies the rural gender/sexual-rights exposure under customary adjudication—but no trans-specific incident, statute, enforcement action, or institutional statement was found for this province. The dossier states plainly: "Free State and Eastern Cape have no trans-specific source at all." Provincial violence against women and girls is severe (multiple 2025 mass-casualty killings in Gqeberha), but arrests followed each incident (four suspects for the May 2025 killings, four for the June 2025 burning of teenagers at KwaNobuhle, charges against a police officer for the July 2025 killings at Gordon Terrace), and none of the victims is identified as trans. The arrests represent a functioning—if strained—state-response mechanism, which is a small positive against the backdrop of extreme national violent-crime rates.

For a visitor, the practical exposure is the general South African violent-crime baseline (national, priced into the 0.69) plus the township-and-rural customary-authority axis where a visibly gender-nonconforming person outside the metro NGO belt is more likely to encounter a chief's moral adjudication than a magistrate's court. No province-level ban, no enforcement against expression, no religious criminal law. The Constitutional Court's Mogale invalidity of the TKLA and the suspended replacement reduce but do not eliminate the parallel-system concern.

records.name: Gauteng
records.summary:
Gauteng — the province containing Johannesburg and Pretoria — is where the country's protections are most visibly operational. It hosts the first representative quantitative study of hate crimes against gay and lesbian people ever conducted anywhere in this country (2003/04, by an LGBT well-being institute with a university applied-psychology centre, documenting prevalence, consequences and contributing factors, with the era's leading community organisations as partners). A 2016 national campaign review confirms only three such studies exist in the country's history, placing Gauteng squarely in the small tier of provinces where the evidence, reporting channels and NGO capacity demonstrably exist. There is no province-specific ban or enforcement action here: the national constitution enumerates sexual orientation, and the equality statute and hate-crime framework operate uniformly, with the courts, prosecutors and civil society that apply them most concentrated in this province.

One caveat cuts both ways: the province's comparatively high recorded hate-crime volume — the very reason the evidence exists — may partly reflect better reporting infrastructure rather than greater danger. The operational conclusion stands either way: an incident a visitor reports here is likeliest to meet a functioning institutional response.

records.name: Western Cape
records.summary:
The Western Cape is the one province the dossier identifies as "usually scored as safest," with the strongest NGO infrastructure and the highest public visibility (Cape Town). No province-specific trans threat, ban, statute, enforcement action, or violent incident was found. For a foreign visitor, the practical implication is that the institutional response to a discovered trans person is a metro court, a PEPUDA-trained magistrate, and a visible civil-society network—the tier of protection that South Africa's constitutional enumeration of gender identity actually reaches in practice. The Hate Crime framework and the constitutional equality clause operate through functioning, accessible metro institutions here more than anywhere else in the country.

One unresolved sub-national question: Khoi-San communities in the Western Cape are pressing for recognition of indigenous authority structures unrecognised for three decades while Nguni chiefs are, with litigation over intangible cultural heritage (Khoin v Jenkins, 2022/2023). This is a parallel-authority recognition question in the safest province, not an existing jurisdiction that adjudicates gender or morality—no chief's court currently operates against a visitor in the Western Cape, and the litigation concerns cultural-heritage recognition, not criminal or moral adjudication of queer people. It is a small uncertainty against an otherwise clean provincial record.

records.name: Île-de-France
records.summary:
Île-de-France sits fractionally below the national 0.67, but the deviation is small because the negative and positive factors largely cancel for a traveller. On the negative side, the Paris agglomeration and urban units over 200,000 inhabitants concentrate 55% of anti-LGBT offences for 43% of the population—a rate of 9 per 100,000, more than double the rural 4 (2025 update: 54% for 43%, still 9 per 100,000 against the rural 4 and national 7). The 2025 Marche des Fiertés was mobilised under a heavy police frame; the self-declared "gay patriot" collective Eros sought to march with prefectural backing, Inter-LGBT threatened to cancel if it participated, and participants reported that "the Marche des fiertés is becoming a sensitive event." A visitor attending the Pride encounters organisational tension and a security apparatus that signals vulnerability even as it protects.

On the positive side, the 9-per-100k rate is heavily inflated by reporting propensity, community visibility, dedicated police liaison desks and the density of associations—all of which mean more incidents are recorded and responded to, not necessarily that a visitor is at greater risk; Paris alone records 22 per 100,000 but the official note cautions that offences there also involve non-residents (commuters and tourists). Île-de-France has the country's densest trans support infrastructure and the largest community, giving a discovered visitor the best odds of institutional help and social buffer anywhere in metropolitan France.
